hints: Focus on the reaction type, heating an organic compound with aqueous NaOH to give a carboxylate salt plus an alcohol means alkaline hydrolysis of an ester.
Notice the two products tell you the two halves, sodium ethanoate comes from a 2-carbon acid part ($\text{CH}_3\text{COO}-$) and hexan-1-ol comes from a straight 6-carbon alcohol part.
Rejoin the pieces as $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_{13}$ and look for the structure with a methyl next to C=O and a straight six-carbon chain attached through oxygen.
walkthrough:
**Recognise alkaline hydrolysis of an ester**

Think of this as splitting an ester with hydroxide. It is a lovely, predictable pattern.

$$\text{RCOOR' + NaOH} \rightarrow \text{RCOONa + R'OH}$$

**Work backwards from the two products**

Sodium ethanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$, tells you the acyl part is $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$, just 2 carbons. Hexan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, tells you the alkoxy part is a straight 6-carbon chain, $\text{-O}(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CH}_3$.

**Rebuild compound X and match the drawing**

Join them back together by removing water logic, acid + alcohol minus water.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH + HO}(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CH}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COO}(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ 
That molecule is hexyl ethanoate, a methyl group attached to C=O on one side and an $\text{-O-CH}_2-$ starting a straight 6-carbon chain on the other. Only one drawing shows exactly that.

options.A: Shows an ethyl ester of a long-chain carboxylic acid (ethyl octanoate type). Hydrolysis would give ethanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, and a long-chain sodium carboxylate, not sodium ethanoate and hexan-1-ol.
options.B: Shows an ethanoate ester, so it would give sodium ethanoate correctly, but the alcohol chain is too long (a 7-carbon heptyl chain). Hydrolysis would give heptan-1-ol, not hexan-1-ol. Classic carbon-counting trap.
options.C: Shows an ethyl ester of hexanoic acid (ethyl hexanoate type). The fragments are the wrong way round. Hydrolysis would give ethanol and sodium hexanoate, not sodium ethanoate and hexan-1-ol.
options.D: Shows $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CH}_3$, hexyl ethanoate. The $\text{CH}_3\text{C=O}$ side gives sodium ethanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$, and the $\text{-O}(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CH}_3$ side gives hexan-1-ol, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{13}\text{OH}$, exactly as observed.
